title: The space between street and door
bodyMd:
Architects like to draw a building as a solid object standing on a plot, but people meet it as a sequence. Between the pavement and the front door lie a series of small stages – a step, a low wall, a gate, a strip of paving – and the character of a street often depends less on its buildings than on how these stages are handled. Planners call the whole sequence the threshold. For decades many of them treated it as waste: a few metres of frontage that could be sold, built over or given to parked cars.

In 2019 a housing cooperative in the town of Castelvera compared two streets built in the same decade with identical dwellings. On Via dei Tigli the houses open directly onto the pavement. On Via Nuova each has a forecourt about three metres deep, with a low wall and a bench. Observers counted how many times, during one week in June, a resident stopped in the street to talk to a neighbour. The count on Via Nuova was almost three times as high, although the street was no quieter and had no more children living on it.

It would be tempting to conclude that forecourts make people sociable. The cooperative's report was more careful. Residents who chose to sit at the front were, it noted, mostly people who already knew their neighbours, and the wall gave them a reason to linger without committing them to a visit. The forecourt did not create friendliness; it lowered the cost of showing it. A resident whose door opens onto the pavement can be seen outdoors only by standing in the doorway, which looks like waiting for a caller. A bench behind a low wall asks nothing of the passer-by, who may nod, stop or walk on.

The lesson for designers is not that every house needs a garden wall. Where land is scarce, as in the older centres of many Italian towns, the same function is served by a doorstep, a bench fixed beneath a window or an arcade that lets a shopkeeper put a chair outside in the rain. What matters is that the threshold offers a place belonging neither wholly to the household nor to the street, where a person can be seen without being obliged to receive anyone. Removing such places to gain floor area may look efficient on paper, but it takes away something that the plans do not measure.
accessibilityText: A four-paragraph essay of about 420 words on the space between a building and the street, which planners call the threshold. The first paragraph says that people meet a building as a sequence of small stages such as a step, a low wall or a gate, and that planners long treated this frontage as waste. The second describes a 2019 comparison by a housing cooperative in the town of Castelvera of two streets with identical dwellings: on one the houses open onto the pavement, on the other each has a forecourt about three metres deep with a low wall and a bench. Observers counted the times a resident stopped in the street to talk to a neighbour during one week in June, and the count on the street with forecourts was almost three times as high, though the streets were equally quiet and had equally many children. The third paragraph warns against concluding that forecourts make people sociable: the report noted that residents who sat at the front mostly already knew their neighbours, so the forecourt lowered the cost of showing friendliness rather than creating it. The fourth paragraph says the lesson is not that every house needs a garden wall, because a doorstep, a fixed bench or an arcade can serve the same function where land is scarce, and that removing such places to gain floor area takes away something plans do not measure.

provenance.notes: Original prose written for this question bank. The town of Castelvera, the cooperative, the two streets and the 2019 survey are invented; the figures are invented too. No published text was copied, paraphrased or reconstructed, and no author is quoted.
